content: Oriental lung fluke disease is caused by more than 30 species of trematodes (flukes) belonging to the genus Paragonimus. Among the species that infect humans, the most common is Paragonimus westermani, also known as the oriental lung fluke. The life cycle of Paragonimus begins when unembryonated eggs are excreted in the sputum or swallowed and passed in the stool. In the external environment, the eggs become embryonated, and miracidia hatch from them. These miracidia actively seek out and penetrate the soft tissues of the first intermediate host, which is a snail. Inside the snail, the miracidia undergo several developmental stages, including sporocysts and rediae, which eventually give rise to numerous cercariae. The cercariae emerge from the snail and invade the second intermediate host, typically a crustacean such as a crab or crayfish. Within the crustacean, the cercariae encyst and develop into metacercariae, which represent the infective stage for mammalian hosts. Humans become infected with Paragonimus westermani by consuming inadequately cooked or pickled crab or crayfish that harbor the metacercariae. Once ingested, the metacercariae excyst in the human host and migrate to the lungs, where they mature into adult flukes. These adult worms measure approximately 5 to 12 mm in length and 4 to 6 mm in width. While the lungs are the primary site of infection, the worms can also migrate to other organs and tissues, such as the brain and striated muscles. However, when this occurs, the life cycle cannot be completed because the eggs laid in these ectopic sites cannot exit the body. The time from infection to egg-laying (oviposition) is approximately 65 to 90 days, and infections can persist for up to 20 years in humans. In addition to humans, animals such as pigs, dogs, and various feline species can also serve as hosts for Paragonimus westermani. The geographic distribution of Paragonimus species is widespread, with infections reported in the Americas, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Paragonimus westermani is predominantly found in Southeast Asia and Japan, while Paragonimus kellicotti is endemic to North America. The clinical features of paragonimiasis vary depending on the phase of infection. During the acute phase, which involves invasion and migration of the parasite, symptoms may include diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, cough, urticaria, hepatosplenomegaly, pulmonary abnormalities, and eosinophilia. In the chronic phase, pulmonary manifestations are more prominent and include cough, expectoration of discolored sputum, hemoptysis, and abnormalities visible on chest radiographs. When adult worms migrate to extrapulmonary sites, such as the brain, the resulting manifestations can be severe and life-threatening. Laboratory diagnosis of paragonimiasis is primarily based on microscopic identification of eggs in stool or sputum. However, eggs are not typically present until 2 to 3 months after infection. In some cases, eggs may also be found in effusion fluid or biopsy material. Concentration techniques may be required for patients with light infections. Biopsy can provide diagnostic confirmation and allow for species identification if an adult or developing fluke is recovered. Diagnostic methods include: Microscopic examination of eggs. Antibody detection, which is particularly useful in cases of light infections and in diagnosing extrapulmonary paragonimiasis. Morphological comparison with other intestinal parasites. The treatment of choice for paragonimiasis is praziquantel. Bithionol is an alternative drug that can also be used to treat this disease.
